meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There are only two plots in all of literature: (1) A person goes on a journey, (2) A stranger comes to town'?
meta.ogDescription: Tolstoy never wrote it. The two-plots adage traces to John Gardner's workshops and a 1986 newsletter; the Tolstoy credit only shows up in 1999.

answer.label: Not Tolstoy — traced to John Gardner
answer.authorDates: 1933–1982 · American novelist and teacher of fiction writing
answer.sourceLine: Tolstoy never wrote this. Quote Investigator traces the saying to the American novelist and writing teacher John Gardner: his posthumous 1984 handbook The Art of Fiction sets a student exercise using “either a trip or the arrival of a stranger,” and from September 1986 writers began quoting Gardner as having said those are the only two plots. QI cautions that no record of Gardner actually saying it has been found — and that the Tolstoy credit, which first surfaces in 1999, is spurious.

source.excerpt: As subject, use either a trip or the arrival of a stranger…
trail: 1984 — Gardner’s posthumous handbook The Art of Fiction: Notes on Craft for Young Writers is published by Alfred A. Knopf (Open Library record ↗). One exercise tells students to write an opening using “either a trip or the arrival of a stranger” — without claiming those exhaust the possibilities (Quote Investigator ↗).

September 1986 — the earliest articulation of the two-plots claim that Quote Investigator located: the writer David Long, in Coda: Poets & Writers Newsletter, reports that Gardner “once observed that there are only two plots” (Quote Investigator ↗).
April 1987 — the novelist Mary Morris repeats it in a New York Times “Hers” column, still crediting Gardner, and the line starts to travel widely (American Dialect Society list ↗).

September 1999 — an article in The Capital Times of Madison, Wisconsin hands the saying to Leo Tolstoy. It is the earliest Tolstoy credit Quote Investigator located, arriving after more than a decade of the line circulating under Gardner’s name (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.cutTag: A writing exercise, not an aphorism
source.excerptNote: This is the passage Quote Investigator identifies as the seed of the adage: an instruction to students in Gardner’s The Art of Fiction, telling them what to write an opening about. QI is careful to note that the exercise never asserts these two possibilities exhaust all plot choices — that leap was made by other people, later.

source.rightsNote: No copyright status can honestly be asserted for the popular one-sentence wording: it has no traceable original text, and it varies from telling to telling — a trip or a journey, a man or a person, comes to town or rides into town. The nearest documented text, John Gardner’s The Art of Fiction (Alfred A. Knopf, 1984), remains in copyright to Gardner’s estate and its publisher, which is why only a short phrase from it is quoted here.

author.name: John Gardner
author.heading: The writing teacher behind the adage
author.bio: John Gardner was born on 21 July 1933 in Batavia, New York, and died on 14 September 1982 in a motorcycle accident in Susquehanna County, Pennsylvania. He is best known for Grendel, which retells Beowulf from the monster’s point of view, and for October Light, which won the National Book Critics Circle Award. He was a lifelong teacher of fiction writing: at Oberlin, at Chico State — where Raymond Carver was among his students — and at San Francisco State, Bennington, Binghamton and the Bread Loaf Writers’ Conference. His two craft books, On Becoming a Novelist and The Art of Fiction, appeared after his death and became fixtures of American writing classrooms, which is very likely how a line from his workshop hardened into an adage.

copyAttribution: "There are only two plots in all of literature: (1) A person goes on a journey, (2) A stranger comes to town." — NOT Tolstoy. No source for it exists in his works, and Quote Investigator calls the Tolstoy link unsupported and apparently spurious. The trail runs through John Gardner's writing teaching: his posthumous handbook The Art of Fiction (Knopf, 1984) sets an exercise using "either a trip or the arrival of a stranger," and the earliest articulation of the two-plots claim that Quote Investigator located is David Long in Coda: Poets & Writers Newsletter, September 1986, crediting Gardner. The Tolstoy credit first appears in The Capital Times of Madison, Wisconsin, in September 1999. Verified at Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Four names, one adage, no source
misattribution.intro: This saying has been handed to a series of increasingly famous writers, and the record shows the handoffs happening in real time.

items.why: The earliest Tolstoy attribution Quote Investigator found is a September 1999 article in The Capital Times of Madison, Wisconsin — more than a decade after the line was already in print under John Gardner’s name. No work of Tolstoy’s has ever been cited as containing it, and QI judges the link “currently unsupported.” (Quote Investigator ↗)

Tolstoy was not even the first Russian to be handed it. In a November 1996 interview in the Cleveland Plain Dealer, the writer and musician Kinky Friedman credited Dostoyevsky with the two-story claim. Same absence of a source. (Quote Investigator ↗)

By 2007 a Sydney Morning Herald writer was hedging across four names at once, naming Gardner, then wondering aloud whether it was Tolstoy, Hemingway or Deepak Chopra. A New York Times piece the same year simply said it had been attributed to everyone from Dostoyevsky to Gardner. (Quote Investigator ↗)

Gardner is where the trail actually leads, and every pre-1996 citation that names anyone at all names him — the one exception in QI’s chronology, an October 1991 Los Angeles Times instance, gives the saying with no attribution. But the exercise in his book only tells students to write an opening using a trip or the arrival of a stranger — it never claims those are the only two plots. QI suggests the adage may be an over-interpretation or misremembering of that exercise, or a remark he made in a classroom that was never recorded. (Quote Investigator ↗)

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that Gardner’s words catalysed the adage but that it is not clear he ever made a matching statement — and that the linkage to Dostoyevsky, Tolstoy and others is “currently unsupported and appears to be spurious.”

context.heading: Why this one spread
lead: It is the perfect workshop line: short, absolute, and flattering to the person repeating it. Every story you can name seems to fit one of the two slots, and the ones that fit both feel like a discovery. That portability is exactly why it drifted — a line this quotable stops needing a source, and the name attached to it keeps getting upgraded.

The upgrade path is visible in the record. Through the late 1980s it is Gardner’s, because people had just read his craft books. By the mid-1990s it is Dostoyevsky’s. By 1999 it is Tolstoy’s. By 2007 a newspaper columnist was listing four possible authors and admitting he could not remember which. Nobody was lying; a good line simply gravitates toward the biggest name in the room.
context.detailsSummary: Two details that give the game away
detailsBody: The wording never settles. Across the citations Quote Investigator gathered, it is a trip or a journey; a man, a person or a friend; a stranger who comes to town or rides into town; two plots, two stories, two themes or two kinds of stories. Genuine textual quotations tend to stabilise around the words on the page. This one behaves like something remembered from a classroom rather than copied from a book.

Even the Gardner attribution got confused. The 2007 Sydney Morning Herald piece calls him “thriller writer John Gardner” — a label that fits not him but his British namesake, the novelist who wrote the continuation James Bond books. By that point the saying had detached from any particular person at all.
context.pull: The adage has a paper trail, and it starts in a 1986 writers’ newsletter — not in nineteenth-century Russia.
